title: Just custom
hook: custom makes anything seem natural, until you travel (Essays 1.23)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the force of imagination: a picture in the mind that the body believes. Your line was it imagines. Did you catch it at work? Day one thousand one hundred fifty.

Shoes off at the door, or shoes on in the house. Dinner at six, or dinner at ten. The fork in the left hand, or switched to the right. A kiss on one cheek, or two, or a handshake. Each of these is, to someone, simply how things are done, so obvious that nobody needs to say it out loud. Then a trip, or a new in-law, or a roommate from somewhere else, and the obvious thing turns out to be a choice. Montaigne wrote an essay about that moment, and he opens it with a woman carrying a calf.
screen: `SHOES OFF, OR SHOES ON.` → `OBVIOUS, TO SOMEONE.` → `A WOMAN CARRYING A CALF.`

segments.voice: First, the story. A village woman, Montaigne tells us, got used to petting and carrying a calf from the day it was born. She kept doing it every day, and because she never stopped, she was still carrying it when it was a full-grown ox. Whoever first told that story, he says, understood the power of custom. It doesn't arrive all at once. It grows a little every day, until we're carrying something enormous without noticing the weight. Second, the schoolmistress. Custom, Montaigne writes, is a violent and sly teacher. She sets up her authority softly, bit by bit, and then shows a tyrant's face, and we no longer dare to raise our eyes to her. Third, the handkerchief. He tells of a gentleman who blew his nose with his fingers and defended it: why, he asked, should we wrap up something dirty in fine linen and carry it around in our pockets? Montaigne admits the argument has some sense to it. Only habit had kept him from seeing how strange the handkerchief is. We notice strangeness in the customs of other countries, he says, and miss it in our own. He goes further: even the rules of conscience, which we say come from nature, are born of custom. Fourth, the brake. Having said all that, Montaigne does not tell anyone to tear up the town's laws. A wise person, he says, should keep their judgment free inside, and outwardly still follow the accepted ways. Questioning a custom and overthrowing it are different things. Day to day, just custom is the pause before calling someone else's way weird.
screen: `A WOMAN CARRIES A CALF, THEN AN OX.` · `CUSTOM, THE SLY SCHOOLMISTRESS.` · `THE STRANGE HANDKERCHIEF.` · `FREE INSIDE, CAREFUL OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `JUST CUSTOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: question one normal thing. Sit and let the breath slow. Then look around the room, or around your day, for one thing you do without ever deciding to. The way you fold towels. Which side of the bed. What counts as being on time. How loud is too loud. Pick one. Ask Montaigne's question, gently: is this nature, or just custom? You don't have to change it. Just see it as a choice for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Just custom. Montaigne's essay on habit: it grows like a calf into an ox, until what we were taught feels like nature, and we only see it when we meet another way. Today's word.
Your line: just custom. Today, when someone does a thing differently from you, before calling it strange, say just custom, and look at your own way once. Day one thousand one hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne take his essay on custom as an invitation to see one's own habits as habits, while noting that he also counsels caution about overturning accepted laws.

what it means: custom grows quietly until it feels like nature, and we see it most clearly in other people's ways.
what a scholar hears: Montaigne pairs this sharp questioning with caution, saying the wise keep judgment free inside while following accepted ways outwardly.

notes: Essays 1.23 (path numbering; 1.22 in some English editions) is paraphrased throughout; confirm all four passages are in this chapter.
The essay's long list of other peoples' customs is deliberately left out so no culture is held up as strange; the hook's examples are everyday and neutral.
'Custom' as 'a violent and sly schoolmistress': paraphrase of 'une violente et traîtresse maîtresse d'école'; confirm.
Original 'maîtresse d'école' is taken from the schoolmistress line; confirm Montaigne's wording and the pronunciation guide.
Editor: the hook's 'woman carrying a cow' corrected to a calf (the essay's story is a calf grown into an ox); varied the stock 'on an ordinary Tuesday' turn.
